---
title: "2. What is AI?"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
---

> Most of what is sold as AI is a function that maps inputs to outputs, fitted
> on examples. That is less magical and more useful than the marketing.

## Learning objectives

1. Use "AI", "machine learning", and "deep learning" correctly.
2. Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and generative tasks.
3. Explain why a model that fits the training data can still be worthless.
4. State what a model cannot tell you, no matter how accurate it is.

## The nesting dolls

These three words are not synonyms.

```
┌─ Artificial Intelligence ──────────────────────┐
│  any system that performs tasks we'd call      │
│  "intelligent" — including hand-written rules  │
│                                                │
│  ┌─ Machine Learning ───────────────────────┐  │
│  │  systems that learn patterns from data   │  │
│  │  rather than being told the rules        │  │
│  │                                          │  │
│  │  ┌─ Deep Learning ───────────────────┐   │  │
│  │  │  ML using many-layered neural     │   │  │
│  │  │  networks. Needs a lot of data.   │   │  │
│  │  └───────────────────────────────────┘   │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

BLAST is arguably AI — it performs an intelligent task using hand-written
rules. It is definitely not machine learning: nobody trained it on examples.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say what you mean
If you fitted a logistic regression, say "logistic regression", not "we applied
AI". Reviewers notice, and precision costs you nothing.
:::

## The three kinds of task

**Supervised** — you have labelled examples and want to predict the label for
new cases. *This sequence is genotype A; that one is genotype D; what is this
new one?* Requires labels, and your model inherits every bias in them.

**Unsupervised** — you have no labels and want structure. *Do these 338 samples
fall into groups?* Nothing guarantees the groups mean anything biological.

**Generative** — you want the model to produce new content: a protein
structure, a plausible sequence, a paragraph of text. Large language models
live here.

| | Needs labels? | Typical question | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised | Yes | "Which class?" | Learns the label's bias |
| Unsupervised | No | "Is there structure?" | Finds structure in noise |
| Generative | Sometimes | "Make me one" | Fluent and wrong |

## The one idea that matters most

A model that performs well on the data it was trained on has demonstrated
nothing. It may have *memorised*.

::: {.callout-important}
## Overfitting
A model with enough parameters can fit any dataset perfectly, including the
noise. It will then fail on new data. The only way to know whether you have
learned a pattern or memorised a table is to test on data the model has
never seen.
:::

The remedy is discipline, not cleverness: split your data before you start,
hold out the test set, and do not look at it until the end. If you tune your
model against the test set, it is no longer a test set.

This is not a technicality. It is the single most common reason published
models fail to replicate.

## What a model cannot tell you

An accurate model tells you two variables carry shared information. It does not
tell you:

- **Which causes which.** Correlation is symmetric; causation is not.
- **Whether a third thing causes both.** This is confounding, and it is the
  subject of the [hands-on case study](../4-hands-on/index.qmd) — where a
  perfectly reasonable analysis produces a result that cannot be interpreted,
  because of how participants were recruited.
- **Whether the question was answerable.** A model always returns a number. The
  number is not a judgement about your study design.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Accuracy is a trap on imbalanced data
If 95% of your samples are HIV-negative, a model that predicts "negative" for
everyone is 95% accurate and completely useless. Always ask what the base rate
is before being impressed by an accuracy figure.
:::

## Check yourself

1. You cluster samples and find three groups. What have you learned?
2. Your classifier is 99% accurate on training data and 60% on held-out data.
   What happened?
3. A tool reports 95% accuracy predicting a condition affecting 5% of people.
   Is it good?

We work through these in the [exercise](exercise.qmd).
